post.title: Uruguay Advances a 500 MW Data Center Campus With 350 MW of Solar
post.content:
Uruguay is coordinating a major digital infrastructure proposal with Spanish renewable energy developer Solaria. On November 9, 2026, the country's presidency confirmed meetings with regional authorities to advance work on a proposed 500 MW data center park and 350 MW of solar generation. The meetings followed an October 14 strategic agreement with Solaria and participation by state electricity utility UTE. Announced investment totals $5.7 billion; completed expenditure and energized computing capacity have not been established.

The developer's announcement describes an initial 200 MW of data center capacity followed by another 300 MW. The first phase would also install the planned photovoltaic generation. Data center development is expected in Canelones and San José, with solar installations in Florida. Government estimates allocate $5.5 billion to digital infrastructure and $200 million to the solar component. Land acquisition, environmental assessment and permitting remain necessary.

Why the 500 kV connection matters

Rather than relying on a dedicated solar array alone, the developer intends to establish a connection to Uruguay's high-voltage transmission system. Solaria would provide land, electrical infrastructure and associated services to computing operators within a free-trade zone. UTE would purchase the photovoltaic electricity under a proposed agreement lasting up to 40 years. The arrangement resembles the coordinated powered-land approach behind Norfolk's solar-backed campus proposal, although each project's commercial and network arrangements differ.

A high-voltage connection allows a large load to exchange power with the wider system while limiting current for a given power transfer. Transformers step down the incoming voltage before distribution to individual buildings, where further conversion supports IT equipment and cooling. Redundant supplies, protection systems and backup generation must be designed around actual reliability requirements rather than the headline connection rating.

Solar capacity does not equal continuous supply

If a 500 MW facility operated at its maximum electrical rating throughout a non-leap year, it would consume 4.38 TWh. A 350 MW solar array operating at an illustrative 20% capacity factor would generate about 613.2 GWh annually, equivalent to 14% of that hypothetical demand. Neither the assumed capacity factor nor the continuous load is a project forecast. Actual generation depends on weather, equipment, losses and curtailment. Solaria says the initial focus is cloud services, with water-efficient closed-loop cooling or equivalent systems. The difference explains why grid access remains important even when generation is developed alongside data centers, as illustrated by Malaysia's solar and storage development and AirTrunk's renewable procurement plans.

At the initial 200 MW scale, the same solar assumption would cover approximately 35% of annual energy demand under continuous full load. Hourly matching would be considerably more complicated because photovoltaic production falls to zero at night. Uruguay's broader electricity portfolio and transmission network could provide complementary supply, but the terms of the proposed procurement and any storage requirements need clarification.

The project strengthens South America's role in energy-oriented digital infrastructure, alongside Paraguay's hydropower-oriented computing infrastructure. Its next meaningful milestones are confirmed site acquisitions, permits, detailed transmission specifications, finalized electricity contracts and construction commitments. The November meetings demonstrate coordination, not completed facilities or operating AI hardware.

post.title: Oracle Contracts Wind Energy From Texas' Operating 300 MW Ranchero Farm
post.content:
Scout Clean Energy announced on October 7, 2026, that Oracle signed a virtual power purchase agreement covering a majority of the electricity produced by the 300 MW Ranchero Wind Farm in Crockett County, Texas. Ranchero entered commercial operation in October 2019. Oracle identifies its Abilene facility as connected to the same ERCOT grid. The agreement changes the commercial allocation of electricity from existing infrastructure rather than establishing a newly built 300 MW facility. Neither the exact contracted share nor the price was disclosed in the announcement.

The agreement forms part of Oracle's broader renewable energy investment in Texas, according to Scout. In a September 15 announcement, Oracle identified more than 1.7 GW of wind generation across ten projects involving multiple developers. The company aims to match its custom AI data center electricity consumption with carbon-free electricity by 2035. A portfolio-wide target should not be confused with demonstrated continuous renewable operation at a particular server campus.

The electrical path from turbines to ERCOT

Scout's Ranchero project profile describes a 345 kV generation interconnection approximately 300 yards long. Turbine generators convert rotor motion into electricity. Collection circuits aggregate their output, and a substation raises the voltage for export. The generation reaches the ERCOT wholesale electricity system rather than a private wire serving Oracle exclusively. Comparable contractual approaches are being considered internationally, including South Africa's renewable wheeling program.

Wind turbines have power curves that depend on wind speed, rotor dimensions and operating controls. Output rises across part of the operating range before reaching rated capacity. At very high wind speeds, protective shutdown can reduce production. Offshore designs such as Scotland's floating wind project face additional installation and maintenance constraints, even when their wind resource is strong.

The economics of a virtual power purchase agreement

A virtual power purchase agreement typically settles the difference between a contracted price and a wholesale reference price without directing physical electricity to the buyer's building. The generator sells power into the market, while the corporate buyer separately procures electricity for its facilities. The contractual treatment of renewable attributes, settlement intervals and price differences depends on the agreement. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's procurement resources explain the structure.

At a hypothetical 40% capacity factor, the entire 300 MW farm would generate 1,051.2 GWh annually in a non-leap year. That equates to an average output of 120 MW, not 300 MW. Oracle's contracted majority would represent a portion of the actual output, which cannot be calculated precisely without the commercial terms. AI installations can draw power continuously, so even a strong annual energy match cannot prove an hourly match.

The distinction also matters for Nova Scotia's proposed wind-backed AI campus and AirTrunk's renewable procurement plans, where future generating capacity and computing loads must be reconciled. Ranchero is already generating electricity, but the commercial agreement does not establish additional installed capacity, incremental emissions reductions or independent round-the-clock supply to Oracle. Actual generation, settlement volumes and retirement of renewable attributes are the next useful metrics.

post.title: Microsoft Builds Auckland Data Center as New Zealand Geothermal Procurement Matures
post.content:
Microsoft has begun building a data center in Westgate, Auckland, expanding its physical infrastructure in New Zealand. A Westgate project overview confirms construction started in September 2026 and identifies piling, excavation, concrete work and crane operations among the activities. The company opened its first hyperscale New Zealand cloud region in December 2024. The new Westgate facility remains under construction; Microsoft has not disclosed its electrical capacity in the reviewed project overview.

The expansion provides a useful example of how a cloud provider can support renewable generation without a dedicated power line between a particular plant and a computing facility. In September 2022 Microsoft signed a ten-year renewable attribute purchase agreement with Contact Energy. Contact disclosed the agreement in May 2023, covering all renewable attributes of its 51.4 MW Te Huka Unit 3 geothermal power station. Contact says the agreement supported its investment decision. Contact subsequently reported through the New Zealand Exchange that the plant came online in December 2024.

Heat beneath the surface

Geothermal electricity uses naturally heated underground fluids. Depending on the reservoir and plant design, steam may drive a turbine directly or transfer heat to a separate working fluid. A generator converts shaft rotation into electrical energy. Returning suitable fluids underground can support reservoir management. Unlike photovoltaic generation, geothermal production is not directly dependent on daylight. Indonesia's geothermal computing study considers a possible direct relationship between geothermal resources and computing in Indonesia.

A 51.4 MW generator operating at rated capacity for 8,760 hours would produce 450,264 MWh in a non-leap year. At an assumed 90% capacity factor, annual production would be approximately 405,238 MWh. The assumed factor is illustrative, not a reported operating statistic for Te Huka. Plant maintenance, reservoir conditions, equipment reliability and dispatch affect real annual output.

Renewable accounting and electrical reliability

Renewable attributes document the environmental characteristics of electricity production. They do not trace individual electrons through a shared transmission network. Contact explicitly describes its contract as an attribute purchase, not exclusive physical electricity delivery to Westgate. The volume assigned to the new facility, if any, and its power requirements are not disclosed. It would therefore be inaccurate to present Te Huka's rating as the data center's dedicated capacity or proof of hourly carbon-free operation.

A cloud campus requires reliable connections, protected distribution equipment, backup capability and cooling systems regardless of its annual renewable procurement strategy. Regional projects including Tasmania's planned AI factories, Sweden's hydropower-oriented AI factory and Paraguay's hydropower-oriented computing infrastructure illustrate how different generation portfolios influence infrastructure planning. Firm renewable output can simplify parts of the energy-matching problem, but reserve requirements and network capacity still matter.

The next verifiable milestones are completed civil construction, electrical commissioning, installed computing capacity and actual operational energy reporting. Microsoft's community explanation describes its long-term regional investment. A construction milestone and a historical geothermal contract are distinct developments; their connection is corporate energy strategy rather than evidence of an exclusive physical power supply.
